posts.title: Your 3am crash isn't weakness
posts.why_shared: Every night worker has felt this; easy 'this is you at 3am' tag for a coworker.
posts.caption: Sleepiness tends to peak between 2 a.m. and 6 a.m., and the end of a night shift is the riskiest time to be behind the wheel (CDC NIOSH). If you're nodding off, pull over or get a ride. When does your crash hit? #nightshift #shiftwork #sleepscience #healthtok #3amcrash

slides.label: The dip
slides.title: Sleepiness peaks from 2 to 6 a.m.
slides.body: That's when your body clock's drive to stay awake is lowest.
slides.source: Source: CDC NIOSH, shift work training

slides.label: The double hit
slides.title: Night shift stacks the deck
slides.body: Sleep pressure builds all shift while your body clock says sleep. Both at once.
slides.source: Source: CDC NIOSH, shift work training

slides.label: Most people miss this
slides.title: The drive home is the danger
slides.body: End of shift is peak sleepiness. Nodding off? Pull over or get a ride.
slides.source: Source: CDC NIOSH, shift work training

slides.text: Night shifters: when does your crash hit?

posts.title: One bad night makes your brain overreact
posts.why_shared: Everyone has a 'snappy when tired' story; invites tagging a friend who is hangry-tired.
posts.caption: In a small brain-scan study, people kept awake overnight showed about 60% more amygdala activity to upsetting images than people who slept (Yoo et al., 2007). What does tired you get annoyed by? #sleep #sleepscience #brain #healthtok #psychology

slides.text: One bad night makes your brain overreact

slides.label: The study
slides.title: 26 adults, one night
slides.body: 14 skipped sleep for a night, 12 slept normally. All then viewed images, neutral to upsetting.
slides.source: Source: Yoo et al., Current Biology, 2007

slides.label: The result
slides.title: Emotional reaction: about 60% stronger
slides.body: Their amygdala, a brain region tied to emotion, responded about 60% more.
slides.source: Source: Yoo et al., Current Biology, 2007

slides.label: The why
slides.title: The brake got weaker
slides.body: Its link to the prefrontal cortex, which helps keep emotions in check, was weaker.
slides.source: Source: Yoo et al., Current Biology, 2007

slides.label: Most people miss this
slides.title: That 'everything is annoying' mood?
slides.body: Short sleep may be part of it. One small study, so it's a clue, not a diagnosis.
slides.source: Source: Yoo et al., Current Biology, 2007

slides.text: What does tired you get annoyed by?

posts.title: Blue-light glasses fix sleep? Not so fast
posts.why_shared: Lots of people own a pair; the 'did yours work?' question splits the comments.
posts.caption: A 2023 Cochrane review found very low-certainty evidence on sleep and low-certainty evidence that blue-light glasses may not ease computer eyestrain (Singh et al.). Did they work for you? #bluelightglasses #sleep #sleepmyths #sleepscience #healthtok

slides.text: Blue-light glasses fix sleep? Not so fast.

slides.label: Sleep
slides.title: Results were mixed
slides.body: 6 trials, 148 people: three found better sleep, three found no difference. Evidence quality: very low.

slides.label: Eye strain
slides.title: Computer eyestrain? Maybe no help
slides.body: 3 trials, 166 people: they may not reduce short-term eyestrain. Low-certainty evidence.

slides.label: Most people miss this
slides.title: 'Unproven' isn't 'useless'
slides.body: The trials were small. Occupational health guidance suggests skipping the computer an hour or so before bed.
slides.source: Source: CDC NIOSH, shift work training

slides.text: Did blue-light glasses work for you?
slides.sub: Yes or no in the comments. Follow for daily sleep science

posts.title: Under 6 hours of sleep: 4x the cold odds
posts.why_shared: A concrete number people repeat to friends who 'run on 5 hours'.
posts.caption: In one study of 164 adults, wrist-tracked sleep under 6 hours was linked to about 4 times the odds of catching a cold after virus exposure, versus 7+ hours (Prather et al., Sleep, 2015). How many hours did you get last night? #sleep #immunity #sleepscience #healthtok #coldseason

slides.text: Under 6 hours of sleep: 4x the cold odds

slides.label: The study
slides.title: 164 adults tracked their sleep
slides.body: A week on wrist trackers. Then cold-virus nasal drops and 5 days in quarantine.

slides.label: The result
slides.title: Short sleepers caught more colds
slides.body: Versus 7+ hours, under 5 hours meant about 4.5x the odds. 5 to 6 hours: about 4.2x.

slides.label: The catch
slides.title: Small study, wide error bars
slides.body: Only 164 people, and the ranges were wide. Treat it as a signal, not a promise.

slides.label: Most people miss this
slides.title: Sleep was tracked before the virus
slides.body: So the virus didn't cause the short nights. Guard your sleep in cold season.

posts.title: Consistent sleep may beat long sleep
posts.why_shared: Challenges the 'just get 8 hours' rule and calls out weekend sleep-ins.
posts.caption: In an observational study of 60,977 UK adults, more regular sleep timing was linked to lower all-cause mortality risk, and regularity predicted it better than sleep duration (Windred et al., Sleep, 2024). How far apart are your weekday and weekend wake times? #sleep #sleepscore #sleepschedule #sleepscience #healthtok

slides.text: Consistent sleep may beat long sleep

slides.label: The study
slides.title: 60,977 adults wore trackers
slides.body: Researchers measured how regular their sleep timing was, then followed them for about 6 years.

slides.label: The finding
slides.title: Steadier sleepers had lower risk
slides.body: The more regular groups had 20% to 48% lower risk of death from any cause.

slides.label: Head to head
slides.title: Regularity beat duration
slides.body: It predicted risk better than hours slept, and hours added little once regularity was counted.

slides.label: The caveat
slides.title: It shows a link, not proof
slides.body: Observational study: people with irregular sleep may differ in other ways.

slides.label: Most people miss this
slides.title: Your weekend wake-up time counts
slides.body: Try keeping it close to your weekday time, then watch your sleep score trend.

posts.title: You're probably eating wrong on nights
posts.why_shared: Night workers will send it to the coworker who lives on vending-machine candy.
posts.caption: Four diet suggestions for night-shift nurses from CDC NIOSH: limit eating from midnight to 6 a.m., keep a normal meal rhythm, skip sugar-rich and low-fiber carbs when sleepy, and eat away from the work site. General guidance, not medical advice. What's your go-to night-shift snack? #nightshift #shiftwork #nursetok #sleepscience #healthtok

slides.text: You're probably eating wrong on nights

slides.label: Mistake 1
slides.title: Heavy eating from midnight to 6 a.m.
slides.body: NIOSH suggests avoiding or reducing food intake in those hours.
slides.source: Source: CDC NIOSH, shift work training

slides.label: Mistake 2
slides.title: Ignoring your normal meal rhythm
slides.body: Stick to normal meal timing as much as you can: three meals per 24 hours.
slides.source: Source: CDC NIOSH, shift work training

slides.label: Mistake 3
slides.title: Sugar and low-fiber carbs for energy
slides.body: They can increase sleepiness. Try vegetables, fruit, yogurt, eggs, nuts, or whole-grain sandwiches.
slides.source: Source: CDC NIOSH, shift work training

slides.label: Most people miss this
slides.title: Eat away from your workstation
slides.body: NIOSH suggests eating with colleagues in a pleasant place away from the work site.
slides.source: Source: CDC NIOSH, shift work training
